name: Adam Ito

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential. Could you start by telling me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for the Ridgeway Electric Co-op, which is the power company owned by the farms and towns it serves out here. I lead a crew of five, and we set poles, string wire and fix whatever the wind knocks down. My uncle Ken taught me the trade, he did thirty-one years on these same lines. I like that I know the people at the end of every wire, I've had dinner in half their kitchens. What wears me out is the young lads who want to be on their phones instead of watching what I'm showing them.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who's at home, and how do things look money-wise?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm engaged to Grace, we get married at our church in June. She works in her dad's hardware store on Main Street. We've got about two months of my pay put away after paying for the ring, and we're saving for a house on her parents' land. I'm a volunteer firefighter too, so between that and storm call-outs, Grace says she's marrying a pager.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here's the card: Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hype. That's what I figured all along.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I've said to anyone who'd listen: the computer people oversold it. At the depot I'd tell the apprentices to put the phones down and learn to tie a proper knot. I don't do social media, so that's that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd think my job's as good as it's ever been. The co-op moves slow, the members want a person they know, and there's always more line to build than men to build it. My uncle Ken climbed these poles for thirty-one years, and I reckon I'll climb them for thirty more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep doing what I do. Get married in June, keep saving, start building the house on Grace's parents' land in a couple of years. I'd take on another apprentice, because the co-op needs more hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Content, really. It's the world I'd want.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does saving look like after the wedding?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About four hundred a month, more in storm season. Grace's dad is giving us the land, so we'd just need enough for the build. I'd do a lot of the work myself with the boys from church.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd worry about even here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The co-op board. A couple of them want to merge with the big city utility to save money. If that happens, we'd be a number in a city office. That worries me more than any computer.

say: I'd say the **computer people** oversold it.
I'd tell apprentices to **put phones down** and learn proper knots.
think: My job is as good as ever because the **co-op** moves slowly.
There's always more line than **men to build** it.
do: **Get married** in June and keep saving.
Build a house on **Grace's parents' land** in a couple of years.
feel: **Calm** and content, the world he'd want.
S0.quote: My uncle Ken climbed these poles for thirty-one years, and I reckon I'll climb them for thirty more.
fieldNote: He takes pride in a **family trade** passed down from his uncle.
His real worry is a **co-op merger** with the city utility.
Community and **church** shape his plans, including building his own house.

steps.text: Keep leading the co-op line crew
Marry Grace at the church in June
Save about four hundred a month for the house build

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Here's the card: Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Planning, booking and answering customers. That's the office. Not my crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's for the office girls and the managers, not for linemen. At the depot I'd say do what you've always done and do it right. If the co-op makes us use a tablet, I'd grumble and use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it barely touches me. The co-op's slow, and the members would complain if a computer answered the phone. The thinking parts of my job, like the job sheets, are maybe an hour a day, and I'd let my second-in-command handle the tablet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going, same as before. Wedding, saving, house. I'd keep an eye on the merger talk, since a big utility would bring in all this faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A computer can answer the co-op's phone, but it won't know that Mrs Hale (an elderly co-op member) needs her power back first because of her oxygen machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd let your second-in-command handle the tablet. Is that a long-term plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Long as it works. Luis is good with that stuff. My job is to know the lines and keep the crew safe. If they made me do it myself, I'd do it, slow and swearing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the co-op merged?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to every member meeting and speak against it first. If it went through anyway, I'd stay, because the work's the work. But I'd be sad about it.

say: I'd say AI is for **the office**, not linemen.
I'd **grumble** but use a tablet if made to.
think: It barely touches me because **the co-op** is slow.
The **job sheets** are only about an hour a day.
do: Keep going with the **wedding, saving and house**.
Watch the **merger talk**, which would speed change.
Speak against the merger at **member meetings**.
feel: **Calm**, mostly, trusting local knowledge over computers.
S1.quote: A computer can answer the co-op's phone, but it won't know that Mrs Hale (an elderly co-op member) needs her power back first because of her oxygen machine.
fieldNote: He sees the thinking parts of his job as **small** and hands them off.
He values **local knowledge** of members, like Mrs Hale's oxygen machine.
The **merger**, not AI, is his main fear here.

steps.text: Hand the tablet job sheets to his second-in-command
Speak against the merger at co-op member meetings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Here's the card: Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2028 and robots by 2031. I'd be married three years, maybe with a little one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a judgement on all of us for putting our trust in machines. At church I'd say we look after each other, like we always have. To the crew I'd say work hard and don't let them say we weren't the best.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the co-op holds out longer than the city folks, but not forever. In 2028 the office goes, and by 2031 a robot can climb a pole as well as me. The board would buy them because it's cheaper. I've got no other trade and I've never wanted one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hold off on having a baby for a year or two, which would be hard on Grace. I'd put every penny into savings. I'd talk to Grace's dad about the hardware store, whether there's room for me to help run it, even if it's less money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be praying a lot. I always thought I'd teach my son to climb like Uncle Ken taught me, and now there might be nothing to teach.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd never wanted another trade. Would you learn the robot side?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe if the co-op paid and it was hands-on. I won't sit at a screen all day. I'd rather sell nails at the hardware store than watch a machine do my work from a truck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you hold responsible?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The tech companies, for selling it before anyone was ready. And folks who think a government cheque fixes everything. A man needs work, not a handout.

say: I'd call it a **judgement** on trusting machines.
At church I'd say we **look after each other**.
think: The co-op holds out longer, but **robots climb poles** by 2031.
I have **no other trade** and never wanted one.
do: **Delay a baby** a year or two.
Ask Grace's dad about helping run the **hardware store**.
feel: **Alarmed** and praying, fearing nothing to pass on.
S2.quote: I always thought I'd teach my son to climb like Uncle Ken taught me, and now there might be nothing to teach.
fieldNote: His **identity** is tied to passing the trade down the family.
He rejects **handouts** and leans on church and in-laws instead.
He'd take **less money** at the store over screen work.

steps.text: Put off trying for a baby for a year or two
Save every spare penny from overtime
Ask Grace's father about a job at the hardware store
Lean on church friends and in-laws for help

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Here's the card: Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, 2031 and 2034. A bit more breathing room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time to get ready, so let's not panic. At church I'd say the same. At the depot I'd keep my head down and do good work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years means the baby and the house can still happen. I'd be thirty-five when robots come. The co-op might keep some of us for the oddball jobs. I'd want to be one of them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build the house on Grace's parents' land in 2028. I'd get my heavy equipment ticket so I can run the digger and the crane, since that's still hands-on. I'd see what happens before changing much else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not lying awake, but it's there. Five years is enough time to build a house and maybe not enough to pay it off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The heavy equipment ticket, is that new for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. Uncle Ken always said a lineman who can run the crane never goes hungry. I'd do it on weekends with a man from church who runs a crane outfit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change your mind about the merger in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. If anything, a local co-op keeps people longer. A city utility would cut first and ask later.

say: I'd say we have **time to get ready**.
At the depot I'd **keep my head down** and work.
think: The **baby and house** can still happen.
The co-op might keep some of us for **oddball jobs**.
do: Build the house on **Grace's parents' land** in 2028.
Get a **heavy equipment ticket** on weekends.
feel: **Anxious**, present but not keeping him awake.
S3.quote: Five years is enough time to build a house and maybe not enough to pay it off.
fieldNote: Five years lets him keep **family plans** on track.
He picks a **hands-on retraining** route through church connections.
He trusts the **local co-op** to protect jobs longer than a city utility.

steps.text: Build the house on Grace's parents' land in 2028
Get a crane and digger ticket on weekends

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Here's the card: Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. 2039 for the robots. I'd be close to forty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, and the Lord provides. At work I'd keep training apprentices. I'd tell Grace not to worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years means I get most of my good years on the poles. I'd still have to find something in my forties, but I'd have the house, the kids, and maybe a ticket or two. The co-op would probably be one of the last to switch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going, get married, have kids, build the house. Get the crane ticket in a few years. Teach my apprentices everything, even if robots come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but only a bit, when I think about the kids growing up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your kids about work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn a trade with your hands and learn to fix things. I'd tell my kids that robots still break, and somebody in this town will have to fix them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still train apprentices, knowing this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. Because even if the job changes, what I teach them is how to work. Turn up on time, check your gear, look after your mates.

say: I'd say ten years is long and **the Lord provides**.
think: I'd get most of my **good years** on the poles.
The co-op would likely be **one of the last** to switch.
do: Get the **crane ticket** in a few years.
feel: Slightly **uneasy**, thinking about his children's future.
S4.quote: I'd tell my kids that robots still break, and somebody in this town will have to fix them.
fieldNote: Ten years lets him live the life he **planned**.
He values teaching **work habits** over specific skills.
His faith gives him **steadiness** about the far future.

steps.text: Keep leading the co-op crew and training apprentices
Start a family and build the house
Get a crane ticket in a few years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. I'd have a young family and a trade nobody needs. What would help is the co-op keeping people on for the odd jobs and paying for hands-on tickets like cranes, and churches and families pulling together. I don't want a government cheque, I want a job where I still get my hands dirty and come home tired.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the storms. When a twister comes through, the whole town goes dark. If the robots aren't there in time, you'd want men like me still around who know where every line runs.

headlineQuote: I don't want a government cheque, I want a job where I still get my hands dirty and come home tired.
portrait: Adam is a **27-year-old crew lead** at a rural power co-op, taught the trade by his uncle.
He is **engaged to Grace**, saving to build a house on her parents' land.
He never uses AI and sees the **co-op merger** as a bigger threat than computers.
He becomes **alarmed** at AGI by 2028, fearing he will have no trade to pass on.
He rejects **handouts** and leans on church, family and hands-on retraining instead.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because he'd have a young family and a trade nobody needs.
whatWouldHelp: The co-op paying for **hands-on tickets** and community support from **church and family**.
